lines.text: A land of copper, great rivers and the mightiest waterfall in Africa. This is the story of Zambia, from its earliest people to today.
About three hundred thousand years ago, an early human lived at Kabwe. A miner found the skull in 1921.
In 1813 David Livingstone was born in Scotland. He would cross central Africa as a missionary and doctor, campaign against the slave trade, and die in Zambia.
In 1855 Livingstone became the first European to see the great falls of the Zambezi. Locally they were the smoke that thunders. He named them for his queen.
Fifty years later, in 1905, a small settlement grew up at Lusaka. It would one day be the capital.
In 1924 Kenneth Kaunda was born. He would lead the struggle for independence and be Zambia's first president.
That same year Britain took over direct rule of Northern Rhodesia from the British South Africa Company.
By the late twenties great copper mines were opening in the north. The Copperbelt would drive the country's fortunes for a century.
In 1955 work began on the Kariba Dam across the Zambezi, holding back one of the largest man-made lakes on Earth.
Hakainde Hichilema was born in 1962. In 2021 he would win the presidency.
In October 1964 Northern Rhodesia became independent as Zambia, with Kenneth Kaunda at its head. He would rule until 1991.
In 1976 a railway built by China opened, linking Zambia's copper to the sea at Dar es Salaam.
From the skull at Kabwe to the thunder of the falls, Zambia's story runs deep.
